title: Harvesting wool from Angora rabbits
subtitle: Plucking or shearing, done at the right time, gives you clean fibre and a calm rabbit.
excerpt: Angora wool grows around 2.5 cm a month. At three months the coat is ready to harvest. Plucking releases naturally moulting fibre; shearing takes everything at once. Here is how to read the coat, choose the method, and collect clean fibre ready for spinning.
sourceNotes: British Angora Goat Society technical notes (adapted for rabbit fibre). British Rabbit Council breed standards for English and French Angora. Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (1994), chapter on fibre animals. Extension service notes from University of Wisconsin on small-scale fibre production.

glossaryTerms.definition: The soft, fine wool harvested from Angora rabbits. Lighter and warmer than sheep wool, it has no lanolin. Sold by the ounce and spun alone or blended.
The natural shedding cycle in Angora rabbits, occurring roughly every three months. During a moult, the coat loosens from the roots and can be plucked free with minimal effort.
The tangling of fibres into a dense, unusable knot. In Angoras it develops quickly if the coat is left ungroomed past the harvest window.

content.text: Angora rabbits grow a coat ready to harvest every three months. Let it go longer and the fibres mat at the root, making the whole thing unusable. Catch it at the right point and the
moulting
coat comes away cleanly in your hand. The choice between plucking and shearing depends on where the rabbit is in its cycle.
Reading the coat

Run your fingers against the growth direction. A coat ready to pluck offers almost no resistance, fibres slide free from the root with light pressure. A coat not yet ready resists and the rabbit will flinch. If it resists, wait another two weeks and recheck.
Look for the break line about 1 cm from the skin where new growth pushes the old coat upward. When the break is clean and the old fibre is uniformly long, the coat is at peak harvest.
Setting up
Work on a table at a comfortable height. Place a clean towel on the surface to collect the fibre as it falls. Have a paper bag or small basket within reach, loose
Angora fibre
floats and collects dust if you leave it in a pile.

Keep the session under thirty minutes. Angoras are calm animals but will become restless and kick if held in one position too long. A kick strong enough to startle you can injure the rabbit's spine if it twists sharply, keep your hold relaxed and supportive, never gripping tightly.
Plucking

Plucking is the preferred method when the moult is running naturally. Take a small pinch of fibres between thumb and forefinger, no more than a teaspoon's worth, and draw them away parallel to the coat in a slow, steady pull. You should feel no resistance.
Start at the back of the neck and work toward the tail in sections. Keep each pinch small.
Transfer each handful to the bag immediately so it doesn't float away.
If you reach an area that resists, skip it and return in a week.
Work the flanks and belly last. The belly is the most sensitive area; keep that session short.
Shearing
Shearing removes the entire coat in one session, useful when the rabbit is not in a full moult but the coat is long enough to risk
matting
. Use small, blunt-tipped animal shears rather than scissors, scissors cut unevenly and risk nicking the skin.
Comb through the coat first to remove any tangles. Work from the outside in.
Hold the shears flat against the skin, cutting parallel to the body surface. The skin on a rabbit is thin and tears easily.
Cut in long strokes from back to front, keeping the coat in one piece where you can, it is easier to grade lengths for spinning if the staples stay aligned.
Leave the belly for last. Stretch the skin gently with your free hand before each cut.
Prime (6 cm+): long clean fibres from the back. Best for spinning fine yarn.
Second (3-6 cm): shoulder and flank fibres, slightly shorter. Good for blending with wool.
Waste (under 3 cm): belly and neck shorts. Useful for felting but hard to spin.
After harvesting
Check the rabbit's skin for any nicks. A small nick from shearing heals on its own; a deeper cut should be cleaned with saline and checked by a vet if it doesn't close within a day.

A freshly sheared rabbit loses heat rapidly. Keep it in a draft-free hutch for the first week and provide additional bedding until the coat begins to grow back. Spring is the best time to shear outdoors precisely because temperatures are rising; a midwinter shear would require indoor housing.

Store the harvested fibre in a paper bag or cotton pillowcase, not plastic, which traps moisture and encourages mildew. Label the bag with the date and the rabbit's name. The fibre keeps for a year or more in dry storage.

attrs.cue: Coat is matted and won't part cleanly
attrs.cause: Left too long past the moult window
attrs.fix: Work dematting comb through the mat section by section. If the mat is tight to the skin, shear it off rather than pulling — pulling causes pain. Plan the next harvest two weeks earlier.

attrs.cue: Rabbit kicks repeatedly and won't settle
attrs.cause: Uncomfortable position or session running too long
attrs.fix: Return the rabbit to its hutch for twenty minutes, then try again. If it is the belly being worked, stop: complete the belly in a separate short session.

attrs.cue: Fibre looks dull and breaks when stretched
attrs.fix: Check the diet for adequate protein and hay. Dull, brittle fibre can signal low protein intake. If accompanied by weight loss or lethargy, have a vet check the rabbit.
